newsitem.title: USA: Intel cuts Pentium prices up to 57 percent. [CORRECTED 23:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Intel cuts Pentium prices up to 57 percent. [CORRECTED 23:40 GMT]

text.p: Intel Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. Monday slashed prices on their best selling computer chips, stepping up their ongoing battle for market share.
Intel, the world's largest maker of computer chips, cut prices on its popular Pentium chips up to 57 percent, prompting Advanced Micro to trim prices on its new K6 chip by as much as 55 percent.

The moves come as Advanced Micro was stepping up efforts to grab customers from Intel with its newly designed and more powerful K6 chip. Analysts said the cuts would help lower personal computer prices later this year.
Intel cut the price of the top-of-the-line Pentium II 300 MHz chip, currently used mainly in engineering workstations, by 57 percent to $851.
The price of the Pentium 233 MHz with MMX chip, one of the most popular models for home and multimedia PCs, was slashed 35 percent to $386.

Intel cuts prices of its chips about once a quarter. Since more than 80 percent of the world's personal computers use Intel chips, the summer price cuts determine PC prices during the crucial back-to-school shopping season.

Analysts have said this summer's price cuts are steeper than usual. Intel wants to move out its older generation of Pentium chips and wants to make its high-speed Pentium II chips more affordable to regular PC users.

"The new prices reflect Intel's continued delivery of increased performance at each price point," Intel said in a statement. The prices became effective for PC makers Sunday, but were officially announced Monday.

Advanced Micro cut the price on its AMD-K6/233 MHz processor to $289 (corrects from $290) from $469, and the price on its AMD-K6/200 MHz to $189 from $349. The price of the AMD-K6/166 MHz is now $109, down from $244.

"This price reduction maintains AMD's strategy of selling the AMD-K6 processor for at least 25 percent less than Intel products at comparable performance levels," said Vinod Dham, group vice president of AMD's Computation Products Group.
"Our value proposition remains unchanged: no matter how much or how little users want to spend for their PCs, they will get higher performance from systems based on the AMD-K6 processor."
AMD said it shipped about 10,000 AMD-K6 units in the first quarter and more than 350,000 AMD-K6 processors in the second quarter. AMD plans to produce more than 1 million units this quarter.
